newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. pilot re-enacts Lindbergh landmark flight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pilot re-enacts Lindbergh landmark flight.

text.p: A 44-year-old Texas businessman paid tribute to aviation pioneer Charles Lindbergh on Wednesday, flying alone across the Atlantic from New York to Paris' Le Bourget air field 70 years after the historic journey.
Bill Signs, flying a 1974 Cessna Centurion at an average speed of 174 mph (277 kph), made the journey of 3,610 miles (5,808 km) in 21 hours, 23 minutes.
It was 11 hours, 54 minutes faster than Lindbergh's 1927 flight of 33 hours 29 minutes, made in a Ryan monoplane dubbed "The Spirit of Saint Louis".

Others have duplicated Lindbergh's solo trans-Atlantic feat, but Signs was the first to begin the adventure, as Lindbergh did, by flying across the United States from San Diego, California, where the Ryan was built.
Both men made stops in Saint Louis, Missouri, and Long Island, New York, before heading alone across the ocean.
Signs' Cessna, made of metal, was heavier than the Ryan, which was built of wood and fabric. Lindbergh's plane also got better mileage.
Signs said he flew at low altitude, "close to the water like Lindbergh did", to prevent the wings of his plane from icing up.
When Lindbergh landed at Le Bourget he was greeted by cheering citizens who had flocked to the airfield outside Paris.

Signs, an auto repair shop owner from Dallas who has flown more than 10,000 hours, was welcomed by school children from the Bourget area, a delegation from the French Women Pilots Association and Le Bourget mayor Frederic Gailland.
Signs said there were no problems on the flight, his longest, but he was a bit embarrassed by the warm welcome.

He made the so-called "Friendship Flight" with the support of dozens of local Texas businesses. He was presented with an emblem of the town of Le Bourget, a copy of Lindbergh's landing authorisation and a replica of the Eiffel Tower.
